title: Sell Mineral Rights in Vance, AL
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Vance, AL | Tuscaloosa County
metaDescription: Own mineral rights near Vance, AL, in southeastern Tuscaloosa County? We check activity near the Black Warrior CBM fairway and make a written cash offer.
heroLead: Vance is best known today for the automotive plant that transformed the town, but the mineral estate underneath much of the area still traces to farmland deeds from long before the plant arrived.
intro: Vance sits in southeastern Tuscaloosa County, close enough to the Black Warrior Basin's coalbed methane fairway that some acreage in the area carries real production history, and far enough on the flank that other tracts nearby have never been leased at all. The town's transformation since the automotive plant opened in the late 1990s changed the surface dramatically, but it didn't change the mineral estate underneath the older farm and timber parcels that surround it.

If your family has held land near Vance for a generation or more, whether it's still farmed today or was sold for industrial and residential development, it's worth confirming what mineral rights, if any, were kept separate.

sections.heading: Industrial growth on top of old farm deeds
paragraphs: The area's rapid industrial and residential growth over the past two and a half decades has pulled in a lot of formerly rural land, and in many of those sales the mineral rights were reserved by the selling family rather than transferred along with the surface. That's a detail that gets lost easily in a fast-moving real estate transaction, but it means a Vance-area mineral interest can survive years or decades after the family stopped farming or living on the land itself.

If you're not sure whether your family's old Vance property carried a mineral reservation, the deed itself will usually say so plainly, and if you don't have a copy we can pull it from Tuscaloosa County Probate Court records.

sections.heading: Proximity to the Black Warrior CBM core
paragraphs: Vance sits closer to the productive core of the basin than many other Tuscaloosa County communities, with the historic Oak Grove and Brookwood coalbed methane fields not far to the northwest. That proximity means it's worth specifically checking whether your parcel falls within a historic or current producing unit rather than assuming based on general location, since unit boundaries in this area can be irregular.

We pull the relevant well and unit records for every Vance-area review, and if your tract has ever been part of a CBM unit, even one that's now largely depleted, that history factors directly into how we price the interest.

sections.heading: What a fair Vance offer looks like
paragraphs: For interests with production history, we weigh recent royalty performance against typical coalbed methane decline behavior in this part of the basin. For acreage that's never been leased, we price against comparable recent Tuscaloosa County transfers and the tract's position relative to the active fairway. Either way, the number we give you comes with a full explanation attached, not a bare figure.

We're also comfortable working with multiple family members if a Vance-area interest has passed through inheritance and is now split among several relatives, which is common for land that's been in a family since before the industrial growth in the area began.

faqs.question: Did the automotive plant development affect mineral rights on nearby land?
faqs.answer: Not directly. Surface development doesn't change mineral ownership, though land sales tied to that growth may have included or excluded mineral reservations depending on how each deed was written, which is why we check the actual document.

faqs.question: Is my land close enough to Oak Grove or Brookwood to matter?
faqs.answer: We check your specific legal description against historic and current unit maps rather than estimating from general location, since the answer varies parcel by parcel even within Vance.

faqs.question: We have an old lease on our land but haven't gotten a check in years. What does that mean?
faqs.answer: It likely means the well or unit has stopped producing or gone into a shut-in status. We can review the lease and any available production records to explain what's happening and what the interest might still be worth.
